title: Position: Artificial Intelligence Needs Meta Intelligence - the Case for Metacognitive AI
claim: Metacognition applies across learning and inference problems, and one concrete mechanism filters unreliable components to improve the shared model.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; (a) stacked topic cards, (b) annotated flow diagram
description: Two-panel figure. Panel (a), on the left, has a large curved blue arrow over a vertical list of three sources of inspiration: metacognitive applications in AI, approaches in science, and cognition in humans. Beside it are two groups of pastel cards. The yellow 'Learning' cards cover learning from limited samples, curriculum and active learning, aggregating decentralized learners, and federated learning. The pink 'Inference' cards cover fast energy-efficient inference, model selection and early stop, partially-observed decision processes, and explore/exploit. Each card has a small icon. On the right, two icon-and-text blurbs map these groups to the FL case. Panel (b) is a flow diagram. Three purple data-source circles (a, b, c) are labeled normal or anomalous and have local-model brain icons. Gray boxes classify each source as trusted or compromised. A blue box gives the monitoring function M(L(θ),φ), and a central aggregation icon sits beside the update equation. A dashed red box at the bottom reads 'Adjusting the aggregation to exclude unreliable clients'. Red devil and X marks and green arrows show rejected versus accepted updates.
caption: Metacognitive approaches in AI for enhanced learning and inference: (a) overview of problems in learning and inference, potential metacognitive solutions, and their realization in the FL case; (b) mechanism of a metacognitive monitoring function (M) within an FL system, illustrating how client trustworthiness evaluation and selective aggregation are used to filter unreliable updates and improve the learning of the global model
abstract: This position paper argues for metacognition as a general design principle for creating more accurate, secure, and efficient AI. The metacognitive solution involves systems monitoring their own states and judiciously allocating resources depending on each problem instance's difficulty or cost of mistakes. Drawing inspiration both from past work on resource-rational AI and from well-documented metacognitive strategies in psychology and cognitive science, we identify specific challenges in embedding these strategies into AI design and highlight open theoretical and implementation problems. We showcase these principles through a tangible example of improved learning efficiency, effectiveness, and security in a Federated Learning (FL) case study. We show how these principles can be translated into practice with a novel software framework developed specifically to allow the community to design, deploy, and experiment with metacognition-enabled AI applications.
